quote: Repay to Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to God.
firstReading: The Lord addresses Cyrus, calling him by name and strengthening him for a purpose Cyrus does not yet fully know. For the sake of Jacob and Israel, God appoints this foreign ruler so that every land may recognize the Lord’s unique sovereignty. There is no god besides the Lord, who forms and sustains his people.
secondReading: Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy greet the Thessalonian church in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. They thank God for faith expressed in action, love revealed in labor, and hope made steadfast in Christ. The community’s election is known because the Gospel arrived not as words alone, but with power, the Holy Spirit, and deep conviction.
psalmSummary: Psalm 96 summons the whole earth to sing a new song to the Lord and proclaim his saving deeds among all peoples. The nations are called to recognize his glory, strength, and kingship, for the idols are nothing while the Lord made the heavens. All creation is invited to worship him in holiness and announce his just reign.
gospelSummary: The Pharisees join with the Herodians in an attempt to entrap Jesus over the imperial tax. They begin with flattering words, then ask whether it is lawful to pay the census tax to Caesar. Jesus recognizes their hypocrisy and asks for the coin used for the tax. Since it bears Caesar’s image and inscription, he directs them to give Caesar what belongs to Caesar and to give God what belongs to God. His answer neither makes political power absolute nor denies its limited claims. Instead, it reveals the prior and comprehensive claim of God upon human beings, who bear the divine image and owe the Lord worship, obedience, and love.
saintReflection: Saint Luke the Evangelist (Feast): Saint Luke, Evangelist and companion of Saint Paul, is traditionally identified as the author of the Gospel according to Luke and the Acts of the Apostles. His two-volume work proclaims the saving mission of Jesus and the Spirit-guided expansion of the Church from Jerusalem to the nations. Luke gives sustained attention to prayer, the Holy Spirit, divine mercy, joy, the dignity of the poor, and the inclusion of those placed at the margins. His Gospel preserves the parables of the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son, as well as scenes in which Mary receives and ponders God's word. Acts shows the risen Christ continuing his work through apostolic witness and ecclesial communion. Luke invites careful listening to Scripture, mercy that crosses boundaries, confidence in the Spirit, and faithful proclamation that salvation in Christ is offered to every people.
dailyPrayer:
Lord God, you alone are God, and there is no other. You guided Cyrus, though he did not know you, so that your people might learn that your saving purpose reaches beyond every boundary. Deliver us from giving any creature the worship, trust, or obedience that belongs to you alone.

Jesus Christ, teach us to recognize your image impressed upon every human person. Purify us from hypocrisy and from words that seek to test rather than receive your truth. Grant us the wisdom to fulfill rightful duties in the world without surrendering our hearts to powers that cannot save.

Through the intercession of Saint Luke the Evangelist, deepen in us love for your word. Make us attentive to the Holy Spirit, steadfast in prayer, merciful toward those at the margins, and joyful in proclaiming salvation to every people. Gather your Church in faithful communion, that our worship may declare your glory among the nations. Amen.
theologicalSynthesis:
Isaiah reveals the Lord as sovereign over history: even Cyrus, a ruler outside Israel, can serve God’s saving design. The passage does not praise human power as ultimate; it declares that the Lord alone is God. Psalm 96 widens this confession into universal worship, calling all nations and creation to acknowledge the Lord’s glory and righteous reign.

In the Gospel, Jesus refuses the false choice posed by his adversaries. Civil authority has a real but limited claim, signified by Caesar’s coin. God’s claim is deeper, because human beings belong to the Creator and bear his image. Christian obedience therefore cannot become idolatry of earthly rule, nor can devotion to God neglect justice and truthful responsibility.

Saint Luke’s witness helps the Church contemplate this universal horizon of salvation. His Gospel and Acts proclaim Christ’s mercy and the Spirit’s work among peoples once regarded as distant. The Lord who directs history calls every nation, every community, and every person to receive the Gospel and render to God the worship that is his due.
exegesis:
Context: Isaiah 45:1, 4-6 stands within the prophet’s proclamation that the God of Israel directs history for the salvation of his people. Cyrus is named as one whom the Lord strengthens and appoints for a particular work. The text is striking because Cyrus is not presented as an Israelite king formed within Israel’s covenantal life. Yet the Lord can employ him for Jacob and Israel. The point is not that Cyrus becomes divine or that political rule possesses sacred ultimacy. Rather, the passage insists that the Lord’s purpose is free, universal, and effective. God acts so that peoples from east to west may know that no god stands beside him.

Context: The reading’s repeated confession of the Lord’s uniqueness gives its theological center. Israel’s God is not one local deity competing for territory or influence. He is the one Lord whose action reaches rulers and nations beyond Israel. Cyrus does not first know the Lord, but the Lord knows, summons, and equips him. This reverses every attempt to make salvation depend upon human possession of power or prior religious standing. The Lord’s election of Israel is ordered toward the manifestation of his name among the nations. God’s fidelity to his people therefore opens outward in a witness to all peoples.

Psalm: Psalm 96 receives this confession and turns it into liturgy. Israel is summoned to sing, bless the Lord’s name, and tell of his salvation day after day. The psalm does not permit worship to remain hidden or narrow. The Lord’s glory is to be declared among the nations, because the gods of the peoples are powerless while the Lord made the heavens. The summons to bring an offering and enter God’s courts acknowledges that worship belongs to the Creator. It is not an ornament added to life; it is the fitting response to the One from whom all things receive being. The psalm also joins worship to judgment: the Lord comes to govern the world with justice and peoples with faithfulness.

Gospel: In Matthew 22:15-21, the Pharisees and Herodians approach Jesus together with a question designed to ensnare him. Their alliance reflects the calculated character of the test. If Jesus rejects the tax, he may be accused before Roman authority; if he simply endorses it, he may appear to betray Israel’s hope. Their opening praise is not reverent faith but hypocrisy, for Jesus immediately exposes their purpose. He asks to see the coin used for the tax. The denarius bears Caesar’s image and inscription, making visible the imperial system behind the question.

Gospel: Jesus’ response establishes an essential distinction without separating the world from God. Caesar may receive what properly pertains to Caesar, but Caesar is not God and cannot claim what belongs to God. The coin bears Caesar’s image; the human person bears God’s image. Thus the final command directs hearers beyond a dispute over currency toward the total claim of the Creator. Worship, conscience, love, and the deepest obedience of the person belong to God alone. Jesus does not authorize contempt for rightful civil responsibilities, but he decisively rejects the idolatrous elevation of earthly authority. Every power is judged by the God whose reign Psalm 96 proclaims and whose providence Isaiah announces.

Saints: Saint Luke the Evangelist leads the Church to contemplate this divine claim through his sustained witness to the saving mission of Jesus and the Spirit-guided spread of the Church. Traditionally identified as the author of the Gospel according to Luke and the Acts of the Apostles, Luke presents salvation moving from Jerusalem toward the nations. This broad horizon resonates with Isaiah’s vision that the Lord’s name be known throughout the earth and with the psalm’s call to proclaim divine glory among all peoples. Luke’s attention to prayer, mercy, the poor, and those at the margins shows what it means for God’s reign to take flesh in the Church. The God to whom all belong gathers those whom human divisions have treated as remote.

Saints: Luke also preserves Mary’s receptive pondering of God’s word and depicts apostolic witness sustained by the risen Christ and the Holy Spirit. These themes illuminate the Gospel’s demand to give God what is God’s. Such giving begins not with empty speech or a test set before Jesus, but with humble listening, worship, repentance, mercy, and proclamation. The Church does not announce a merely private devotion. In communion, she bears witness that Jesus Christ is Lord and that salvation is offered to every people. Luke’s proclamation resists exclusion, because the Lord’s mercy crosses boundaries and the Spirit forms one people from many nations.

Today: The readings call the faithful to examine every allegiance before the sovereignty of God. It is possible to fulfill temporal duties while allowing created powers, public approval, wealth, or fear to occupy the place owed to the Lord. Jesus’ answer forbids such worship. Those baptized into Christ belong first to God and must allow that belonging to shape prayer, moral truth, mercy, and service of neighbor. Psalm 96 gives the proper posture: reverent adoration before the Lord who reigns. With Saint Luke, the Church receives Scripture carefully, relies on the Holy Spirit, and announces with joy that the one God seeks the salvation of all peoples.
